newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Air CEO doesn't see big changes to plan.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Air CEO doesn't see big changes to plan.

text.p: Canadian Airlines Corp. Chief Executive Kevin Benson moved on Thursday to stem speculation the company would overhaul its survival plan after talks with its major unions.

Canadian and its unions said after a meeting in Vancouver on Wednesday that the talks were constructive on various issues surrounding the carrier's life-support plan. The parties agreed to meet again next week after reviewing the new ideas.
But in a message to employees on Thursday, Benson said the company would not consider fundamental changes to its three-pronged strategy, despite media speculation to the contrary.
"I remain convinced that the basics of the plan as discussed with you, including the 10 percent salary and wage reduction, are essential to return this company to long-term profitability," he said.
The company said it was premature to comment on the level of flexibility it was prepared to show on the plan.

Peggy Nash, who coordinates collective bargaining with Canadian Airlines for the Canadian Auto Workers union and was a union delegate to the meeting, said, however, that Benson was willing at least to discuss alternatives for the company's survival.
One topic explored by Canadian and union leaders on Wednesday was the concept of some reregulation of Canada's domestic airline industry, Nash said.

Benson said before Wednesday that the survival plan's main initiatives, which include employee wage cuts, major route restructurings and a C$48 million ($36 million) cut in fees paid annually to AMR Corp., parent of American Airlines, were not negotiable. AMR owns 33 percent of Canadian.
"My impression yesterday was they were discussable," Nash told Reuters on Thursday.
"Our position has always been that we have to sit down and have some dialogue here. Our view on the cutbacks on the wages has not changed, but we believe that we have some other ideas to offer."
The CAW and the 5,300-member International Association of Machinists have both rejected the company's call for wage cuts, saying staff paychecks were not the cause of Canadian's financial woes.

Nash said the CAW and other unions presented the case that restricting the frequency of flights, fares and new entrants into the industry within Canada would lead to better returns for the ailing carrier, which has not posted an annual profit since 1988.

Analysts have said that one of the main problems in Canada's domestic air industry has been crippling overcapacity, which Canadian said it would address by cutting unprofitable routes and using smaller aircraft on others.

"We're not saying lock it up tight -- we're saying look at where some of the problems are and let's see if there's a role for government to step in and try to at least, where there are problems, provide some stability," she said, adding that restrictions on the right to fly to various cities work well for international flights.

Canadian Transport Minister David Anderson said in Vancouver on Thursday that he did not know of any stipulations in the Open Skies treaty between Canada and the United States that would preclude government intervention.
